note: Two instantiations per unit, one in baking and one in carpentry. copied_runs counts consecutive words, function words included, against the whole paper.

instantiations: In order to better feed the family, home cooks are always looking to study old loaves in order to develop reliable baking habits.
In order to better keep a frame square, woodworkers are always looking to study old joints in order to develop reliable shop habits.

In this note, we bring in the old habits of a bakery based on the doughs we have kept, and use a small trial to settle the best amounts for each one, and subsequently build a weekly bake from them on this basis.

In this note, we bring in the old habits of a workshop based on the boards we have kept, and use a small trial to settle the best sizes for each one, and subsequently build a weekly job from them on this basis.
An improved baking plan based on a longer rest and a cooler oven is then proposed.
An improved shop plan based on a longer dry-fit and a lighter clamp is then proposed.
We screened the slow fold, the poke test and other dough based decisions about when to bake.
We screened the slow cut, the flex test and other board based decisions about when to glue.
Firstly, aiming at the tallest loaf, a small trial for settling the best amounts of a recipe is set up by using the dough of the first week, and these best amounts are worked out by hand.
Firstly, aiming at the stiffest frame, a small trial for settling the best sizes of a joint is set up by using the boards of the first week, and these best sizes are worked out by hand.
The bakes found that: in the wheat, the slow fold and the long rest give plainly better loaves than the fast mix and the cold proof under the best amounts of a single recipe.
The builds found that: in the oak, the slow cut and the long dry-fit give plainly better frames than the fast cut and the cold glue under the best sizes of a single joint.
Through the recipe we found that the opening scoop of flour across one week ended up as a full rack of loaves and a steady weekly count.
Through the joint we found that the opening stack of boards across one week ended up as a full order of frames and a steady weekly count.
Subsequently, to improve the timing of the bake, we use a rest chart to read the dough ahead, and use those readings in the working out of the fold count.
Subsequently, to improve the timing of the glue, we use a fit chart to read the board ahead, and use those readings in the working out of the cut count.
By improving we found that the opening scoop of flour across one week ended up as a fuller rack with a steadier weekly count which is well ahead of the earlier bake.
By improving we found that the opening stack of boards across one week ended up as a fuller order with a steadier weekly count which is well ahead of the earlier build.

We also look at whether the recipe is the one to keep and find that sound habits can lift the bake by looking at the sense of the habits, the working out of the best amounts, and the tall loaves the recipe gives.

We also look at whether the joint is the one to keep and find that sound habits can lift the build by looking at the sense of the habits, the working out of the best sizes, and the stiff frames the joint gives.

In addition to this, using a tally that pretends the cook already knows every rise of the week to reach its best loaf and its best count, we find that the fullest rack under that pretence is far beyond us and the best count our recipe managed was only a sliver of it.

In addition to this, using a tally that pretends the maker already knows every fit of the week to reach its best frame and its best count, we find that the fullest order under that pretence is far beyond us and the best count our joint managed was only a sliver of it.
But it is still far better than the well known bakeries in town.
But it is still far better than the well known workshops in town.

To better understand the effect of oven heat on a single habit or on the whole bake, we look at the change in loaves and in the number of bakes for a single habit and for the whole bake, respectively, when the oven heat changes.

To better understand the effect of clamp time on a single habit or on the whole build, we look at the change in frames and in the number of glue-ups for a single habit and for the whole build, respectively, when the clamp time changes.
It is found that a rise in oven heat for a single habit leads to fewer loaves, some habits show a sharp drop in the number of bakes as the heat rises, and some habits show a gentle drop.
It is found that a rise in clamp time for a single habit leads to fewer frames, some habits show a sharp drop in the number of glue-ups as the time rises, and some habits show a gentle drop.
This indicates that our bake is more even overall and has a clearer edge compared with a single habit.
This indicates that our build is more even overall and has a clearer edge compared with a single habit.
For home cooks the matter of a weekly loaf.
For home woodworkers the matter of a square frame.
On the one hand, cooks keep turning the dough over and over in order to get a taller loaf and fewer sunk ones, which leads to an overworked dough.
On the one hand, makers keep planing the same joint over and over in order to get a tighter fit and fewer loose ones, which leads to an overworked joint.
On the other hand, cooks have to spend fuel on every bake, and the two doughs, wheat and rye, also behave differently through the day.
On the other hand, makers have to spend blades on every cut, and the two boards, oak and pine, also behave differently through the season.
Considering the kitchen notes and the limits set out in the order, we need to settle the following questions.
Considering the shop notes and the limits set out in the job, we need to settle the following questions.
By writing a recipe and writing the best baking habit from the dough already on the bench, and using the written habit and recipe to work out the loaves from the opening scoop a week on.
By writing a joint and writing the best shop habit from the boards already in the rack, and using the written habit and joint to work out the frames from the opening stack a week on.
Task 1: requires writing a recipe and a best habit and working out the loaves after one week.
Task 1: requires writing a joint and a best habit and working out the frames after one week.
In this note, the dough based decision about when to bake is screened.
In this note, the board based decision about when to glue is screened.
The rest chart is then used to work out the fold count using the readings taken ahead and adding a safeguard of pulling the loaf early.
The fit chart is then used to work out the cut count using the readings taken ahead and adding a safeguard of easing the clamp early.

This note first looks at the sense of the habits chosen and then sets them against the loaves of a cook who already knew every rise and the loaves of the good bakeries to show the recipe is the one to keep.

This note first looks at the sense of the habits chosen and then sets them against the frames of a maker who already knew every fit and the frames of the good workshops to show the joint is the one to keep.
This note watches the change in loaves and the change in the number of bakes through the change in oven heat, and looks at the effect of oven heat on the bake.
This note watches the change in frames and the change in the number of glue-ups through the change in clamp time, and looks at the effect of clamp time on the build.
Assumption 1: the dough has no smallest scoop.
Assumption 1: the board has no smallest offcut.
The smallest scoop of flour is a pinch, but this is a small share of the batch, so this note assumes that there is no smallest scoop of flour.
The smallest offcut of timber is a shaving, but this is a small share of the stack, so this note assumes that there is no smallest offcut of timber.
Home baking is open to ruined batches, such as a dough that collapses in the tin, and we have written our recipe to not consider the possibility of such bad batches happening.
Hand work is open to ruined joints, such as a board that splits along the grain, and we have written our joint to not consider the possibility of such bad joints happening.
The main names used in this note are set out in the chart.
The main names used in this note are set out in the chart.
In a home kitchen, cooks can judge a dough from outside signs such as the weather and the clock, but this is only a rough reading at a glance.
In a home workshop, makers can judge a board from outside signs such as the weather and the season, but this is only a rough reading at a glance.
Since the oven is cold in the morning, there is a lack of a warm tin.
Since the shop is damp in winter, there is a lack of a dry board.
For this, we use the warmth of the tin from the day before as the warmth for the morning.
For this, we use the dryness of the board from the day before as the dryness for the morning.
Since the cue each habit we chose mostly follows is the spring of the dough, the borrowed warmth will not affect the reading of the habit.
Since the cue each habit we chose mostly follows is the flex of the board, the borrowed dryness will not affect the reading of the habit.

It has been found that in a bakery, there is a steady link between certain signs and the loaf that comes out over a given stretch, and such signs can help us choose a dough or decide when to start and stop, we call them cues.

It has been found that in a workshop, there is a steady link between certain signs and the frame that comes out over a given stretch, and such signs can help us choose a board or decide when to start and stop, we call them cues.
The poke test, the window pane and the sag are spring cues, the fold count, the rest and the oven spring are pace cues, and the crust is a limit cue.
The flex test, the knock and the gap are fit cues, the cut count, the dry-fit and the clamp are pace cues, and the finish is a limit cue.
The sag, or the drop of the dough, uses two rests of different lengths to judge how lively the dough is now and how it will bake.
The gap, or the play in the joint, uses two fits of different lengths to judge how tight the joint is now and how it will hold.
In the first two lines, the mark is the height of the dough that morning. The two counts are the number of folds in the long rest and the short rest, which are amounts to be settled.
In the first two lines, the mark is the width of the board that morning. The two counts are the number of passes in the long fit and the short fit, which are sizes to be settled.
When the sag is greater than the line, it is a bake; conversely, when the sag is less than the line, it is a wait.
When the gap is greater than the line, it is a glue; conversely, when the gap is less than the line, it is a wait.
The amounts used for a plain loaf for each habit are not necessarily right for the wheat and the rye.
The sizes used for a plain frame for each habit are not necessarily right for the oak and the pine.
In the bake above, the tally is the fullest rack across the week.
In the build above, the tally is the fullest order across the week.

In addition, folding the whole batch when it climbs is more rewarding, and holding the whole batch when it sinks wastes less, so we assume that a fold takes the whole batch and a wait holds the whole batch.

In addition, cutting the whole stack when it closes is more rewarding, and holding the whole stack when it opens wastes less, so we assume that a cut takes the whole stack and a wait holds the whole stack.
As the chart can be read, the best amounts are a handful of folds, a deep rest and a hot oven, for a tall loaf.
As the chart can be read, the best sizes are a handful of passes, a long dry-fit and a firm clamp, for a stiff frame.
The bake as a whole in the best-amount case is better, a good way ahead of the uncorrected one, which shows that the tuning of the amounts works.
The build as a whole in the best-size case is better, a good way ahead of the uncorrected one, which shows that the tuning of the sizes works.
By counting how many cues say to bake the wheat or the rye, a bake is started when the number of cues saying so for either dough reaches a few or more.
By counting how many cues say to glue the oak or the pine, a glue-up is started when the number of cues saying so for either board reaches a few or more.
When both the wheat and the rye say bake, or one says bake and the other is already rising, the split-by-score tally is used to work out the shares of both for moving dough between tins.
When both the oak and the pine say glue, or one says glue and the other is already clamped, the split-by-score tally is used to work out the shares of both for moving boards between clamps.
In the first recipe we use the cues of this morning to decide whether a bake happens the next morning.
In the first joint we use the cues of this morning to decide whether a glue-up happens the next morning.
To lift the bake further, we bring in a dough reading that uses the cues of the next morning to decide whether a bake happens that same morning.
To lift the build further, we bring in a board reading that uses the cues of the next morning to decide whether a glue-up happens that same morning.
A safeguard can better cut the losses from a collapsed dough and thus raise the reward of the bake.
A safeguard can better cut the losses from a split board and thus raise the reward of the build.
Therefore, we put a hard stop into the weekly bake to force the loaf out of the oven when the sag reaches a set mark.
Therefore, we put a hard stop into the weekly build to force the joint out of the clamp when the gap reaches a set mark.
The longer rest and the safeguard used in the new bake gave a rack that stood well above the rack of the first bake, with a good result.
The longer dry-fit and the safeguard used in the new build gave an order that stood well above the order of the first build, with a good result.
The habits we have chosen are widely used in bakeries and are habits with a sound basis that serve well in home baking.
The habits we have chosen are widely used in workshops and are habits with a sound basis that serve well in hand work.
Let us suppose there are cooks who can see the whole week ahead and already know every rise of the wheat and the rye for the coming days.
Let us suppose there are makers who can see the whole week ahead and already know every fit of the oak and the pine for the coming days.
We ran the tally above on paper and reached a fullest rack, of which the best count from the recipe we wrote was only a sliver.
We ran the tally above on paper and reached a fullest order, of which the best count from the joint we wrote was only a sliver.

Although the weekly counts of the bakeries are worked out after dropping costs such as wages, while our weekly counts carry none of those costs, the counts of the recipes we wrote are in most weeks higher than those of the two bakeries.

Although the weekly counts of the workshops are worked out after dropping costs such as wages, while our weekly counts carry none of those costs, the counts of the joints we wrote are in most weeks higher than those of the two workshops.

Cases such as the long rest are mainly due to the rise in oven heat lifting the bar for starting a bake, while cases such as the slow fold are mainly due to their own habit of being fussy and slow to answer.

Cases such as the long dry-fit are mainly due to the rise in clamp time lifting the bar for starting a glue-up, while cases such as the slow cut are mainly due to their own habit of being fussy and slow to answer.
This is because a rise in oven heat will inevitably lead to more cautious baking, which will affect the rack.
This is because a rise in clamp time will inevitably lead to more cautious cutting, which will affect the order.
Our bake is more even overall and has a clearer edge over any single habit.
Our build is more even overall and has a clearer edge over any single habit.
Every one of us hopes to learn from old loaves so as to gain baking habits that can lead to a fuller rack.
Every one of us hopes to learn from old frames so as to gain shop habits that can lead to a fuller order.
The above then makes an improved weekly bake, and our bake is set out as follows.
The above then makes an improved weekly build, and our build is set out as follows.
With the recipe and habit we wrote, we reckoned that the opening scoop of flour across one week finishes as a full rack, with a daily count and a weekly count, which is good.
With the joint and habit we wrote, we reckoned that the opening stack of boards across one week finishes as a full order, with a daily count and a weekly count, which is good.
These are the results of our baking on the matter of a weekly loaf for home cooks, and we sincerely hope they will be of use to you.
These are the results of our woodwork on the matter of a square frame for home makers, and we sincerely hope they will be of use to you.
